subject: Post-demo: request/response boundaries, streaming & auth clarifications
messages:
From: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek@redwood.com>

Cc: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com>, Laura Bennett <laura@redwood.com>

Subject: Post-demo: request/response boundaries, streaming & auth clarifications

Samir / Nadia —

Thanks again for your time today. Quick recap and the technical questions we promised to follow up on from the demo so your engineering team can scope the PoC: 

1) SDK/auth: you asked about best practice for authenticating server-side vs client-side. Recommendation: server-side API keys for backend-only inference (rotate using KMS, short-lived ephemeral keys for transient agents). If you need browser-based flows, front the client with a short-lived session token issued from your backend; avoid embedding permanent keys in the client. We attached a short quickstart (redwood_sdk_quickstart.md) that shows an auth handshake pattern and examples for Node and Python.

2) Request/response contract: you raised structured output and tool calling. Use the chat endpoint for structured tool-calling and function/schema enforcement (messages + function_definitions). Completions endpoints can still work for single-turn prompt->response patterns but lack the structured function calling surface.

3) Tokenization & max_tokens: remember the token budget is prompt (including system + context) + completion. For PoC, conservative defaults: max_tokens = 512 for reply; model-dependent — for larger context models bump up. We also suggested using prefix caching for repeated prompts to reduce usage.

4) Stop sequences & streaming semantics: when streaming is enabled, stop sequences may arrive mid-stream; clients should handle early termination (stop signal) and close the stream gracefully. We recommend sending explicit stop tokens in structured outputs (e.g., '\n\n### END###') to make delimiters deterministic in streaming.

5) Routing & fallbacks: for latency-sensitive endpoints, we recommend primary routing to hosted low-latency model and fallback to a cheaper dedicated variant for burst protection. We'll include an example routing policy in the Drive link.

Next steps:
- Ben to provide a compact PoC checklist (auth snippet + example chat schema + streaming example) — attaching quickstart and a mock schema.
- OmniHealth to confirm target dataset size and latency SLOs so we can size Dedicated slots if needed.
- Aim to kick off PoC next week if your infra team can sign off on the onboarding doc.

— Vivek
Vivek Kulkarni
Enterprise Sales, Redwood Inference

Vivek — thanks for the recap and the quickstart. A couple clarifying questions from our lead engineer: 

1) For the chat endpoint, are message objects tokenized on the server exactly as they appear (so system+user+assistant tokens are additive)? We want to verify how conversation history affects prompt tokens when we have long medical notes.

2) Streaming: If we stream partial tokens for an assistant reply, is there a finalization event that guarantees the completion exceeded stop sequences? Essentially, can a stream be truncated and not contain the stop marker?

3) Embeddings + reranker: when you recommend generating dense embeddings for reranking, should we send the full patient note or chunk by section? What's the recommended chunk size for semantic coherence vs cost?

We could do a short technical sync with Ben and a member of your infra team — can we get 30 minutes tomorrow?

— Samir

CTO, OmniHealth AI

> On Tue, Jun 8, 2026 at 19:02 Ben Carter <ben@redwood.com> wrote:
> > Samir / Vivek / Nadia — quick answers ahead of tomorrow's sync and the PoC checklist attached.
> > 
> > 1) Tokenization: yes, the server tokenizes the whole concatenated message set (system + history + user) using the model's tokenizer; tokens are additive. For long medical notes we recommend chunking by section with semantic boundaries (e.g., HPI, Meds, Vitals). Typical chunk sizes: 500-1200 characters (~200-600 tokens) works well for embeddings and preserves coherence.
> > 
> > 2) max_tokens: set to expected reply length + safety margin (we typically use 512 for most single-turn responses). For streaming interactive agents, keep max_tokens lower (256-512) and re-open new requests for follow-ups to avoid runaway costs.
> > 
> > 3) Streaming & stop semantics: the stream emits token deltas and a terminal event when generation finishes. However, stop sequences can cause early termination; the final event may not include a literal stop token in the final chunk if the stop is handled server-side (the stream will close and include a finalization frame). Clients should rely on the 'done' event/frame rather than searching for a textual stop in the last chunk. Our SDK examples show a 'on_end' callback to mark completion.
> > 
> > 4) Embeddings & rerankers: chunk patient notes at semantic boundaries. For reranking, generate embeddings for the candidate responses and the document chunks; we recommend 128-512 token chunks depending on your average section length. Also recommend a hybrid approach: recover top-K by embedding similarity, then rerank with a lightweight fine-tuned reranker or the scoring endpoint (cheap, low-latency).
> > 
> > 5) Auth patterns / PoC: for the PoC start with server-side API keys and short TTL tokens for any client interactions. We'll provide sample code in the quickstart.
> >
